source.title: Learning Trajectories are Generalization Indicators
source.authors: Jingwen Fu; Zhi-Zheng Zhang; Dacheng Yin; Yan Lu; Nanning Zheng

record.tranche_reason: The paper mentions double descent as background, but its own results study trajectory-based generalization estimates rather than testing any of the listed double-descent versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites double descent in the introduction. Its experiments examine a trajectory-complexity term and generalization-error proxies under training, label-noise, and learning-rate changes; they do not sweep model size, test for a fall-rise-fall in test error, or locate an interpolation peak.
record.test_reason: Double descent appears only as one introductory citation (ref [6], Belkin et al.) motivating the work. The experiments do not sweep model size, sample size or regularization, and do not look for a fall-rise-fall in test error. They test whether a trajectory-complexity term C(Jt) tracks a generalization-error proxy over training and under label-noise and learning-rate changes. 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses', since the paper does no analysis of double descent beyond the one citation.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors also propose a trajectory-based generalization bound that is tighter than stability bounds on a toy example (3.62 vs 4.04 against a true gap of 1.49). They add that Assumption 3.4 holds unless training overfits extremely.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops and evaluates a trajectory-based generalization bound; it does not reproduce the original double-descent experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported trajectory-term/generalization-proxy relationship is examined under changes to learning rate and label-noise level; the text says the learning-rate trend is captured when the rate is small.

fits_no_version.finding: The trajectory term C(Jt) tracks a gradient-based generalization-error proxy over training on VGG13/CIFAR-10. It also rises with label noise and tracks the learning-rate trend at small learning rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A learning-trajectory complexity term can track generalization-error changes during SGD training and under label-noise and learning-rate changes.

record.problems: The study does not directly test double descent. Its relevant experimental outcomes are described as trends without numerical values in the text; Figure 3 averages three experiments per data point, and no uncertainty estimates are stated.

untested.parts: All: no model-size sweep or interpolation threshold.
All: test error over epochs is not examined for a fall-rise-fall shape.
All: no capacity sweep across model classes.
All: C(Jt) is a trajectory-complexity term but is not used to predict peak locations.
Label noise is varied, but not in relation to a double-descent peak, multiple peaks or tuned regularization.

record.verdict_notes: The relation is changed from discusses to cites_only, because double descent appears only as one introductory sentence citing Belkin et al. The tranche stays T6. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size sweep, interpolation threshold, and fall-rise-fall test-error shape.
The study tracks a generalization-error proxy during training but does not test for epoch-wise fall-rise-fall test error.
No sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.
No capacity sweep across model classes or interpolation-point analysis.
The study proposes a trajectory-complexity term but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
Label noise is varied, but the study does not test its effect on a double-descent peak, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.

rows.subject: VGG13
rows.operation_detail: Compared the trajectory term C(Jt) with an approximate generalization-error signal during training.
rows.measure: Trend of C(Jt) versus ∇FS′(Jt)−∇FS(Jt), used as an approximate generalization-error signal
rows.value: The paper reports similar trends after the early stage of training.
rows.note: This is a trajectory-proxy comparison, not a test of epoch-wise double descent.
rows.check: Compares the proposed term C(Jt) with a gradient-gap proxy over training. It is not a test-error-over-epochs curve, so it says nothing about epoch-wise double descent. The link to none is correct.

rows.subject: VGG13
rows.operation_detail: Measured approximate generalization error across varied label-noise levels.
rows.value: Both the generalization error and C(Jt) increase as label noise is raised.
rows.note: The paper gives the trend but no numerical values for the noise levels or outcomes in the text.
rows.check: Reports a generalization-error proxy rising with label noise, with no size or capacity axis and no peak, so it bears on no version. The link to none is correct. Noise levels are not stated.

rows.subject: VGG13
rows.operation_detail: Measured C(Jt) across varied label-noise levels.
rows.value: C(Jt) increases as label noise is raised.
rows.note: The study relates this measure to generalization error but does not measure a double-descent peak.
rows.check: This is the paper's own bound term, not a rate of the behaviour. It is arguably a method-output row rather than a finding; keep it only as context.

rows.subject: VGG13
rows.operation_detail: Measured the relationship between C(Jt) and approximate generalization error across learning rates.
rows.value: C(Jt) captures the generalization-error trend when the learning rate is small.
rows.note: The text does not give the learning-rate values or a numerical trend.
rows.check: Concerns how well the method tracks error across learning rates. Learning-rate values are not stated and there is no double-descent measure.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
